analysis.one_liner: Lets tipped workers deduct their reported cash tips from federal income tax.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously on May 20, 2025, with 8 cosponsors from both parties, but the House has held it at the desk without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let workers in jobs that customarily get tips deduct up to $25,000 in reported cash tips from their federal taxable income each year, without having to itemize deductions. The break phases out for people who earned above a set threshold (about $160,000) from that employer the year before, and it only counts tips a worker reports to their employer for tax purposes. It also expands an existing business tax credit that reimburses employers for payroll taxes they pay on employee tips, adding salons, barbershops, nail salons, and spas to the list of covered businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers — servers, bartenders, delivery drivers, hairstylists, and others — who currently pay federal income tax on tips even though the money goes straight into their pockets. A full-time server making $40,000 in reported tips could reduce taxable income substantially, worth thousands of dollars a year. Employers in the beauty industry also gain a new payroll-tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tipped workers like servers and stylists

how_it_helps.text: Creates a deduction of up to $25,000 per year for qualified tips, which lowers the federal income tax a tipped worker owes on that income.
The deduction is available even to workers who take the standard deduction rather than itemizing, so it reaches most tip earners.
The break is targeted: workers who earned more than a set threshold (about $160,000 in 2025) from the employer cannot claim it, so the benefit is aimed at middle- and lower-income tip earners.
Extends the existing employer credit for payroll taxes paid on tips to beauty services — barbering and hair care, nail care, esthetics, and spa treatments — reducing those employers' tax bills.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced federal revenue, since income that is currently taxed would no longer be. Workers in non-tipped jobs get no comparable break, and only cash tips that are reported to the employer count.

drawbacks.text: Only cash tips count, and only if the worker reports them to their employer for payroll-tax withholding as the law already requires — so tips left as non-cash items or never reported get no benefit.
High earners are excluded: anyone who made more than the threshold (about $160,000) from that employer in the prior year cannot claim the deduction.
The expanded employer credit is a direct tax cut for salon and spa owners, layered on top of the worker deduction, and the bill changes how the credit amount is calculated for those businesses.

Because a deduction reduces taxable income, every dollar deducted is revenue the federal government does not collect, adding to the deficit unless offset elsewhere — a cost that applies to all taxpayers, not just tip earners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tipped workers it covers, this is real and immediate relief: several thousand dollars a year for a full-time server or stylist. The design is narrower than the name suggests — cash tips only, reported tips only, high earners excluded — so many gig and delivery workers with mixed or unreported tips benefit less or not at all. The main honest objections are the revenue cost to the Treasury and that the bill singles out tipped workers for a tax break that other low-wage workers doing similar work cannot get. The expanded employer credit is a business tax cut that does nothing directly for workers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously by voice consent in May 2025 and sent it to the House, where it has been sitting at the desk with no vote scheduled since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 16, 2025 and referred to the Finance Committee.
The Finance Committee was discharged from the bill on May 20, 2025, allowing the Senate to consider it without a formal markup.
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on May 20, 2025 — no roll-call vote was taken.
The House received the bill on May 26, 2025 and held it at the desk; no further House action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has won yet, because the bill has not become law. If the House passes it, tipped workers and beauty-industry employers gain; if it stalls, the status quo — tips fully taxed — continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — no final vote in the House

industries.industry: Beauty and personal-care services (salons, barbershops, nail salons, spas)
industries.note: These businesses win twice: their workers get the new tip deduction, and the employers themselves get a newly expanded credit for the payroll taxes they pay on tips. The employer credit lowers business costs without directly touching workers' pay.

The bill does not change their existing employer credit, but by making tip income tax-free it strengthens the tipped-wage model in which restaurants pay a lower base wage and customers' tips make up the difference. Servers gain real tax relief at the same time.

analysis.trajectory: The House has taken no action since holding the bill at the desk in May 2025. A deduction for tips on essentially the same design was enacted in mid-2025 through a larger tax-and-spending law, so the House may treat this standalone bill as redundant and simply let it expire at the end of the Congress — the usual fate for a Senate-passed bill the other chamber never votes on.
